newsitem.title: USA: Six states may join against Staples merger.
newsitem.headline: Six states may join against Staples merger.

text.p: Six states Friday considered joining the federal government's effort to stop the merger of office superstore chains Staples and Office Depot, as the case got its first airing in federal court.
Appearing before Federal District Court Judge Thomas Hogan, Federal Trade Commission lawyer Melvin Orlans said individual states were examining the possibility of entering the case.
Maryland, New York, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia and Washington State filed affidavits with the court, seeking documents to help them decide whether to join the suit.
The FTC had gone to court seeking a 10-day temporary restraining order to prevent the two chains from merging immediately.
Staples and Office Depot deflected the move by promising to remain separate for now and pledged to tell Hogan and the government if they change their minds.
At issue before Hogan is whether he should grant the government a preliminary injunction, which would prevent a merger so long as legal wheels grind in the case.
Federal Trade Commission chief litigator George Cary asked the judge to grant the preliminary injunction based on written arguments and affidavits from both sides.
Cary said the documents show the cut-throat competition between Staples and Office Depot.

"They talk about how hard it is to achieve pricing parity with Office Depot and the effect it had on their profit margins," he said of some Staples documents. "They're trying to run away from their documents."
If the preliminary injunction is granted the next step would be an administrative trial before the FTC where the case would be argued on its merits, Cary said.
But Donald Kempf, lead attorney for the office superstores, argued for a full-blown 10-day hearing before Hogan with witnesses from both sides.
He argued top executives of the companies would put the paper in perspective. Kempf said that while many people put many things on paper, decisions were made by those at the top.
Beyond that, Kempf argued that federal court was the arena for testimony because the next stage would never be reached.
"The reality is that if a preliminary injunction is entered in this case there will never be an adminsitrative hearing," he said. "The deal will abort."
Cary said that was beside the point.

"If the parties decide not to proceed that should not be the criteria for deciding whether to grant a preliminary injunction," he told Hogan, adding that an administrative trial on the merits of the case would last 5 1/2 months from start to finish.

Hogan asked for further written briefs and set another hearing for Monday at 9:30 a.m. Office Depot stock was off 50 cents at $14.125 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, while Staples stock was down 37.5 cents at $21.125.
